Introduction and Learning Objectives¶

This notebook introduces generalized disjunctive programs through an example in Pyomo.GDP. Students will learn concepts related to Logical Modeling and Modeling Disjunctions in this notebook. These techniques will be applied to the Reactor Problem and then implemented into Pyomo. Critical thinking discussion questions will be included to connect concepts from CBE 60499.

Motivating Example: Separation¶

The following excerpts are from Section 15.7 in Biegler, Grossmann, and Westerberg (1997).

From Integer Programs, we saw that modeling “choose only 1 item” is straightforward:

∑i∈Ryi=1 \sum_{i \in R} y_i = 1 ∑i∈R​yi​=1

Let’s consider something more complex:

“If the absorber to recover the product is selected or the membrane is selected, then do not use cryogenic distillation.”

Yes/No binary decisions:

  • yAy_AyA​: absorber

  • yMy_MyM​: membrane

  • yCSy_{CS}yCS​: cryogenic separation

How to translate this logical statement into a linear constraint?

Click here to see answer

One option:

yA+yM+2yCS≤2 y_A + y_M + 2y_{CS} \leq 2 yA​+yM​+2yCS​≤2

Another option:

yA+yCS≤1 y_A + y_{CS} \leq 1 yA​+yCS​≤1

yM+yCS≤1 y_M + y_{CS} \leq 1 yM​+yCS​≤1

They are equivalent, but the latter is “tighter”; it constrains more of the feasible space. (Think of 3D visualization.)

We seek a formal system to go from logical statements to linear constraints.

Logical Modeling¶

First we will look at important logic notation that is commonly used in logical modeling. This will enable us to convert logical expressions such as disjunctive clauses (Qi=P1∨P2 ∨...∨ PrQ_i = P_1 \lor P_2 \ \lor ... \lor \ P_rQi​=P1​∨P2​ ∨...∨ Pr​) into conjunctive normal form (Q1∧Q2 ∧...∧ QsQ_1 \land Q_2 \ \land ... \land \ Q_sQ1​∧Q2​ ∧...∧ Qs​).

Symbolic Logic Notation¶

Logical OperationLogical Symbol
OR\text{OR}OR∨\lor∨
AND\text{AND}AND∧\land∧
IMPLICATION\text{IMPLICATION}IMPLICATION⇒\Rightarrow⇒
NEGATION\text{NEGATION}NEGATION¬\neg¬
EQUIVALENCE\text{EQUIVALENCE}EQUIVALENCE⇔\Leftrightarrow⇔
EXCLUSIVE OR\text{EXCLUSIVE OR}EXCLUSIVE OR⊻\veebar⊻

Vocabulary¶

Literal PiP_iPi​ is a selection or action and yiy_iyi​ is the associated binary (true/false) variable:

yi={1if Pi is true0otherwise y_i = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if~} P_i \text{~is~true} \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}yi​={10​if Pi​ is trueotherwise​

Negation or complement ¬Pi\neg P_i¬Pi​ implies 1−yi1 - y_i1−yi​.

Conjunctive normal form: sequence of clauses connected by AND operators

Atom or atomic formula: no deeper structure (e.g., no connectives or subformulas)

Literal: atom or its negation

Conjunctive clause: finite collection of literals connected with ∧ \wedge ∧. (The clause is true when all literals are true.)

Disjunctive clause: finite collection connected with ∨ \vee ∨. (The clause is true when at least one literal is true.)

Example: Qi Q_i Qi​ is a disjunctive clause, P1∨P2∨⋯∨Pr P_1 \vee P_2 \vee \dots \vee P_r P1​∨P2​∨⋯∨Pr​, such that y1+⋯+yr≥1 y_1 + \dots + y_r \geq 1 y1​+⋯+yr​≥1.

Need a system to convert logical statements into conjunctive normal form, e.g., Q1∧Q2∧...∧QnQ_1 \wedge Q_2 \wedge ... \wedge Q_nQ1​∧Q2​∧...∧Qn​

Logical Statements and Conjunctive Normal Form¶

The following excerpts are from Section 15.7 in Biegler, Grossmann, and Westerberg (1997).

The three step procedure below shows how to convert logical statements into conjunctive normal form:

Step 1: Replace the implication by its equivalent disjunction. Example:

P1⇒P2⇔¬P1∨P2(15.18)P_{1} \Rightarrow P_{2} \Leftrightarrow \neg P_{1} \lor P_{2} \tag{15.18}P1​⇒P2​⇔¬P1​∨P2​(15.18)

Example: Separation Sequence¶

Let’s revisit the example from the top of the notebook. Reformulate:

PA∨PM  ⟹  ¬PCSP_A \lor P_M \implies \neg P_{CS}PA​∨PM​⟹¬PCS​
(5)

Step 1:

¬(PA∨PM)∨¬PCS\neg (P_A \lor P_M) \lor \neg P_{CS}¬(PA​∨PM​)∨¬PCS​
(6)

Step 2:

(¬PA∧¬PM)∨¬PCS(\neg P_A \land \neg P_M) \lor \neg P_{CS}(¬PA​∧¬PM​)∨¬PCS​
(7)

Step 3:

(¬PA∨¬PCS)∧(¬PM∨¬PCS)(\neg P_A \lor \neg P_{CS}) \land (\neg P_M \lor \neg P_{CS})(¬PA​∨¬PCS​)∧(¬PM​∨¬PCS​)
(8)

Now substituting:

¬PA→1−yA,¬PCS→1−yCS \neg P_A \rightarrow 1 - y_A, \quad \neg P_{CS} \rightarrow 1 - y_{CS} ¬PA​→1−yA​,¬PCS​→1−yCS​

¬PM→1−yM,¬PCS→1−yCS \neg P_M \rightarrow 1 - y_M, \quad \neg P_{CS} \rightarrow 1 - y_{CS} ¬PM​→1−yM​,¬PCS​→1−yCS​

We get:

(1−yA)+(1−yCS)≥1 (1 - y_A) + (1 - y_{CS}) \geq 1 (1−yA​)+(1−yCS​)≥1

(1−yM)+(1−yCS)≥1 (1 - y_M) + (1 - y_{CS}) \geq 1 (1−yM​)+(1−yCS​)≥1

Rearrange:

yA+yCS≤1 y_A + y_{CS} \leq 1 yA​+yCS​≤1

yM+yCS≤1 y_M + y_{CS} \leq 1 yM​+yCS​≤1

Example: Assembling Components¶

If you use (parts 1 and 2) or part 3, then you must also use parts 4 or 5.

PiP_iPi​ true means “use part iii” (corresponding to yiy_iyi​).

(P1∧P2)∨P3  ⟹  (P4∨P5)(P_1 \land P_2) \lor P_3 \implies (P_4 \lor P_5)(P1​∧P2​)∨P3​⟹(P4​∨P5​)
(9)

Step 1:

¬((P1∧P2)∨P3)∨(P4∨P5)\neg ((P_1 \land P_2) \lor P_3) \lor (P_4 \lor P_5)¬((P1​∧P2​)∨P3​)∨(P4​∨P5​)
(10)

which simplifies to:

¬(P1∧P2)∧¬P3∨(P4∨P5)\neg (P_1 \land P_2) \land \neg P_3 \lor (P_4 \lor P_5)¬(P1​∧P2​)∧¬P3​∨(P4​∨P5​)
(11)

Step 2:

(¬P1∨¬P2)∧¬P3∨(P4∨P5)(\neg P_1 \lor \neg P_2) \land \neg P_3 \lor (P_4 \lor P_5)(¬P1​∨¬P2​)∧¬P3​∨(P4​∨P5​)
(12)

Step 3:

(¬P1∨¬P2∨P4∨P5)∧(¬P3∨P4∨P5)(\neg P_1 \lor \neg P_2 \lor P_4 \lor P_5) \land (\neg P_3 \lor P_4 \lor P_5)(¬P1​∨¬P2​∨P4​∨P5​)∧(¬P3​∨P4​∨P5​)
(13)

We now have our statement in conjunctive normal form.

On the left of the ∧\land∧ is equivalent to:

(1−y1)+(1−y2)+y4+y5≥1(1 - y_1) + (1 - y_2) + y_4 + y_5 \geq 1(1−y1​)+(1−y2​)+y4​+y5​≥1
(14)

Simplifying:

−y1−y2+y4+y5≥−1-y_1 - y_2 + y_4 + y_5 \geq -1−y1​−y2​+y4​+y5​≥−1
(15)

Rearranging:

y1+y2−y4−y5≤1y_1 + y_2 - y_4 - y_5 \leq 1y1​+y2​−y4​−y5​≤1
(16)

On the right of the ∧\land∧ is equivalent to:

(1−y3)+y4+y5≥1(1 - y_3) + y_4 + y_5 \geq 1(1−y3​)+y4​+y5​≥1
(17)

Simplifying:

y3−y4−y5≤0y_3 - y_4 - y_5 \leq 0y3​−y4​−y5​≤0
(18)

Modeling Disjunctions¶

When modeling disjunctions, we will have to represent logical constraints that involve continuous variables.

Example: The Reactor Problem¶

The following excerpts are from Section 15.8 in Biegler, Grossmann, and Westerberg (1997).

This modeling disjunctions example involves selecting between two reactors:

  • If reactor 1 is selected, then pressure PPP must be between 5 and 10 atmospheres.

  • If reactor 2 is selected, then pressure PPP must be between 20 and 30 atmospheres.

Linear Disjunction Form:

∨i∈D[Aix≤bi]\lor_{i \in D} \begin{bmatrix} A_{i}x \leq b_{i} \end{bmatrix}∨i∈D​[Ai​x≤bi​​]
(20)

Applied to the Reactor Problem:

[y1P≤10−P≤−5]∨[y2P≤30−P≤−20]\begin{bmatrix} y_1\\ P \leq 10\\ -P \leq -5 \end{bmatrix} \lor \begin{bmatrix} y_2\\ P \leq 30\\ -P \leq -20 \end{bmatrix}⎣⎡​y1​P≤10−P≤−5​⎦⎤​∨⎣⎡​y2​P≤30−P≤−20​⎦⎤​
(21)


where y1y_{1}y1​ represents reactor 1 and y2y_{2}y2​ represents reactor 2.

Define Model in Pyomo with GDP¶

First we will define the model (including disjunctions) for the Reactor Problem in Pyomo.

"""
Instead of using
# import pyomo.environ as pyo
We can import specific functions/objects
"""

from pyomo.environ import (
    check_optimal_termination,
    ConcreteModel,
    Param,
    Set,
    SolverFactory,
    TransformationFactory,
    Var,
)
def create_model():
    """
    Build the reactor problem model.

    Return:
    model: Pyomo model

    """
    ## Model
    model = ConcreteModel(name="Selecting a reactor")

    ## Sets
    # Initialized for reactor 1 (1) and reactor 2 (2)
    model.reactors = Set(initialize=[1, 2])

    ## Parameters
    # Initialized with a dictionary where the keys are 1 and 2 (the reactors)
    # for the minimum and maximum pressure values (atm)
    model.min_pressure = Param(model.reactors, initialize={1: 5, 2: 20})
    model.max_pressure = Param(model.reactors, initialize={1: 10, 2: 30})

    ## Variables
    # Reactor pressure bounded between the lower bound (5 atm) and upper bound (30 atm).
    # These bounds are what gdp.bigm reads to compute M per row -- here 20, 0, 0, 15.
    # It cannot transform an UNBOUNDED variable, so the bounds are not optional.
    model.P = Var(bounds=(5, 30), doc="Reactor pressure (atm)")

    ## Adding an objective for the example
    @model.Objective()
    def objective(b):
        return b.P

    ## Disjunction
    # ONE disjunction over the reactors. Each DISJUNCT is itself a list -- the
    # two pressure bounds that hold together when that reactor is selected.
    # Note: Pyomo.GDP by default treats the disjunction as a xor (choose only one),
    # i.e. it adds sum(y_i) == 1 for you.
    # Notice what is NOT written anywhere below: no big-M constant, and no binary
    # y_i. Both are produced later, by whichever transformation you apply.
    # https://pyomo.readthedocs.io/en/latest/modeling_extensions/gdp/modeling.html
    @model.Disjunction(
        doc="Select exactly one reactor; each brings its own pressure window"
    )
    def pressure_bounds(b):
        # The nesting matters: a list OF lists. Flattening this into a single
        # list would declare a different disjunction -- four one-constraint
        # alternatives instead of two two-constraint ones.
        return [
            [b.P <= b.max_pressure[r], b.P >= b.min_pressure[r]] for r in b.reactors
        ]

    return model
Warning

The nesting matters. @model.Disjunction returns a list of disjuncts, and each disjunct is itself a list of constraints that hold together. Here that is a list of two lists: one per reactor, each carrying both of that reactor’s pressure bounds.

Flatten it, or index the decorator over model.reactors, and Pyomo builds a different model. Indexing over the reactors gives two disjunctions --- “for reactor 1, either P≤10P \leq 10P≤10 or P≥5P \geq 5P≥5” and “for reactor 2, either P≤30P \leq 30P≤30 or P≥20P \geq 20P≥20” --- neither of which restricts PPP at all, since P∈[5,30]P \in [5, 30]P∈[5,30] already satisfies one branch of each. That model admits P=15P = 15P=15, which the disjunction forbids.

It is worth knowing that this error is invisible in the answer below: the objective is min⁡P\min PminP, and both the right model and the wrong one return P=5P = 5P=5. Check a model by asking what it excludes, not only what it returns.

Transform and Solve with Big-M Relaxation¶

The following excerpts are from Section 15.8 in Biegler, Grossmann, and Westerberg (1997).

Use “Big-M” constraints to convert linear disjunctions into mixed-integer constraints to represent logic with continuous variables.

Big-M Relaxation Approach¶

General Notation:

Aix≤bi+Mi(1−yi) , ∀i∈DA_{i}x \leq b_{i} + M_{i}(1-y_{i}) \ , \ \forall i \in DAi​x≤bi​+Mi​(1−yi​) , ∀i∈D
(22)
∑i∈Dyi=1\sum_{i \in D} y_{i} = 1i∈D∑​yi​=1
(23)
yi∈{0,1} , ∀i∈Dy_{i} \in \{0,1\} \ , \ \forall i \in Dyi​∈{0,1} , ∀i∈D
(24)

Applied to the Reactor Problem:

P≤10+M1(1−y1)−P≤−5+M1(1−y1)P≤30+M2(1−y2)−P≤−20+M2(1−y2)y1+y2=1P \leq 10 + M_{1}(1-y_{1})\\ -P \leq -5 + M_{1}(1-y_{1})\\ P \leq 30 + M_{2}(1-y_{2})\\ -P \leq -20 + M_{2}(1-y_{2})\\ y_{1} + y_{2} = 1P≤10+M1​(1−y1​)−P≤−5+M1​(1−y1​)P≤30+M2​(1−y2​)−P≤−20+M2​(1−y2​)y1​+y2​=1
(25)

When the yyy’s are considered continuous variables, weak bounds for the objective function are formed for large values such as:

M1=100  and  M2=100M_{1} = 100 \ \ \text{and} \ \ M_{2} = 100M1​=100  and  M2​=100

Main Idea: Considering the special case where hi(x)=Aix−bi≤0,h_{i}(x) = A_{i}x - b_{i} \leq 0,hi​(x)=Ai​x−bi​≤0,
MiM_{i}Mi​ is sufficiently large to relax hi(x)≤0h_{i}(x) \leq 0hi​(x)≤0 when yi=0y_{i}=0yi​=0

Key Takeaways:

  • If MMM is too large, we can get a “weak relaxation” because integer programming algorithms need more iterations.

  • If MMM is too small, we can get unintended bounds.

Big-M is the best to use if the problem is small.

Transform and Solve with Convex Hull Relaxation¶

The following excerpts are from Section 15.8 in Biegler, Grossmann, and Westerberg (1997).

Convex hull can be used if we don’t want to implement Big-M parameters. This approach requires separating the continuous variables into its components.

Convex Hull Relaxation Approach¶

General Notation:

x=∑i∈Dzix = \sum_{i \in D} z_{i}x=i∈D∑​zi​
(26)
Aizi≤biyi , ∀i∈DA_{i} z_{i} \leq b_{i}y_{i} \ , \ \forall i \in DAi​zi​≤bi​yi​ , ∀i∈D
(27)
∑i∈Dyi=1\sum_{i \in D} y_{i} = 1i∈D∑​yi​=1
(28)
0≤zi≤Uyi , ∀i∈D0 \leq z_{i} \leq Uy_{i} \ , \ \forall i \in D0≤zi​≤Uyi​ , ∀i∈D
(29)
yi∈{0,1} , ∀i∈Dy_{i} \in \{0,1\} \ , \ \forall i \in Dyi​∈{0,1} , ∀i∈D
(30)

ziz_{i}zi​: continuous variables separated into as many new variables as there are terms for the disjunctions.

Applied to the Reactor Problem:

P=P1+P2P1≤10y1P2≤30y2−P1≤−5y1−P2≤−20y2y1+y2=1P = P_{1} + P_{2} \\ P_{1} \leq 10y_{1}\\ P_{2} \leq 30y_{2} \\ -P_{1} \leq -5y_{1}\\ -P_{2} \leq -20y_{2}\\ y_{1} + y_{2} = 1P=P1​+P2​P1​≤10y1​P2​≤30y2​−P1​≤−5y1​−P2​≤−20y2​y1​+y2​=1
(31)

Key Takeaways:

(+) Constraints do not require Big-M parameters which produce a tight linear programming relaxation.
(--) A larger number of variables and constraints is required.

Convex hull is better to use over Big-M if the problem is large.

Convex Hull Implementation in Pyomo¶

We will repeat the procedure above but using Convex Hull now.

model = create_model()

assert check_optimal_termination(results), (
    f"Solve failed: status={results.solver.status}, "

Discussion Questions¶

  1. How do we create a system to go from logical expressions to linear constraints?

  2. Are conjunctive or disjunctive clauses more common? Why might this be the case?

  3. If yi=0y_{i}=0yi​=0 or yi=1y_{i}=1yi​=1, what happens when a Big-M parameter is introduced in the general notation?

  4. When will the convex hull formulation simplify?

Click to see the ideas for the discussion questions

  1. Using conjunctive normal form.

  2. Disjunctive clauses because the clause is true when at least one literal is true which occurs more often.

  3. The inequality becomes unnecessary when yi=0y_{i}=0yi​=0 and the inequality is applied when yi=1y_{i}=1yi​=1.

  4. If the disjunction only has two terms and one of the terms requires the variable to take a value at 0.
